cim: AI’s biggest effects in the Berkshires might be hiding in plain sight
cim_eredeti: AI’s biggest effects in the Berkshires might be hiding in plain sight
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence is already shaping your weather forecasts, hiring, banking, healthcare and business visibility across the Berkshires, often without you realizing you are interacting with it.

So much of the conversation about artificial intelligence is about "big": big money, big data centers, big changes, big danger, big personalities, big impacts, big ideas.

But “big” only tells part of the story. “Big” only exists when it's been absorbed into the lives of individuals and their communities.

An imperfect analogy: What made Big Tobacco big? The fact that tens of millions of people smoked cigarettes and spent their money to buy them.

Cigarettes shaped our concept of “cool” and influenced our media and culture. Automakers installed cigarette lighters in cars. Restaurants had smoking — and nonsmoking — sections.

Note to readers: AI and Us is the first in a three-part series by Gerol Petruzella, a philosopher-technologist and an academic technology consultant at Williams College, exploring artificial intelligence’s impact in the Berkshires. Today’s column examines how AI is changing the businesses, organizations and systems that support our communities. The second will explore its effects on daily life, including learning, relationships and social habits. The third will examine what makes the technology different and what is profit-driven hype.

The series kicked off with a preview article, "AI is changing our world. First, let's understand what it is," which set the table for this series.

Even if you didn’t smoke — and separate from moral judgments about smoking — Big Tobacco had an effect on us all. Today’s “big” AI is already on track for similar economy-wide, and culture-wide, impacts.

I grew up in Pittsfield and have made my life and career in the Berkshires. In my experience with AI safety research, alignment (ensuring AI acts in humans’ interests), benchmarking (measuring how skilled new models are) and higher education, I've worked with nonprofits, AI developers and government agencies.

But I'm interested in what AI means at the local level — its implications for the towns we live in, the diners we eat at, the schools we send our kids to, the town halls we visit, the local farms where we stop on Saturday morning to pick up zucchini.

AI impacts the systems and sources of information we rely on — systems and sources used by local organizations, whether they be businesses or municipal governments.

Are you a farmer in Becket relying on weather forecasting? AI models like Google's WeatherNext 3 are under the hood of weather apps.

Where traditional forecasting models require hours on supercomputers to run, today’s AI creates detailed local forecasts on ordinary hardware at speed. It’s a game-changer in dangerous weather conditions where minutes count or in places where geography creates micro-climates — such as when there is heavy rain in North Adams, while just a few miles east, Florida has sunny skies.

Google DeepMind: The PodcastCan artificial intelligence solve one of science’s most chaotic physics puzzles? In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry sits down with Peter Battaglia, Senior Director of Research at Google DeepMind, to explore how machine learning is transforming global weather forecasting. (Sept. 9, 2026)

Large farms are already using AI-driven systems for “precision agriculture,” reducing water and fertilizer use and costs — techniques likely to arrive soon for smaller regional farms in our area.

AI-powered tools like Flock cameras — capable of tracking a car’s travel through license plate recognition — promise local police critical information for public safety by tracking the movements of suspects. (The accuracy — and costs — of that promise are separate questions.)

How does your credit union or bank keep current on financial information? Morningstar, Reuters, Bloomberg and other major financial news sources already include AI in the services they provide to professional financial customers like banks and financial advisors.

Another important but invisible influence: AI shapes how local organizations manage their day-to-day work.

Washington Post video: Research teams across the United States are leading the charge in finding ways to reduce disease and increase yields at the nation's farms through AI.

Some of these tools are in use; others are being developed. Supply chains and distributors are a big deal for small businesses, especially in rural areas like ours.

The next time your mechanic has to order brake calipers, how do they know that they'll show up on Thursday instead of in two weeks? An AI model predicted how many of that part should be stocked in our area, ready for delivery.

Sysco, the food distributor, uses SAGE (Sysco Agentic Ecosystem) for inventory management and demand forecasting.

Town road crews trying to keep up with pothole patching on a thin budget? Tools like PaveX use sensors under cars to scan the pavement for cracks and potholes, giving an AI model the data to track and prioritize repair needs accurately.

Applying for jobs? The hiring platforms that businesses large and small use to rank and reject candidates incorporate AI.

Healthcare is no exception: Berkshire Health Systems actively pilots the use of AI “scribes” to capture audio and transcribe it into clinical notes.

AI is changing communication and advertising — a significant shift for a region whose economy depends heavily on tourism.

The advice that small businesses absorbed in the 2010s was to build a website, post on social media and learn search engine optimization. This described a ladder that rewarded effort.

But unlike Google search, AI has no "page two."

In other words, if one asks Gemini, Google’s AI assistant, for a good Italian restaurant in Pittsfield, you may get five suggestions, rather than several pages of links to explore.

Fewer than a third of Google searches now send a click anywhere, and the smallest sites (hence, the small businesses) are absorbing most of that loss.

Whether a Lenox inn surfaces in a chatbot's answer depends largely on how much has already been written about the Berkshires, which means 90 years of Jacob's Pillow coverage and 25 years of Mass MoCA coverage are deep in ChatGPT's training data.

Our cultural institutions have quietly become the region's citation infrastructure — the digital “shape” of the Berkshires trained into an AI's depiction of the world.

That doesn't mean AI touches everyone the same way. Someone who's come to Tanglewood every summer for 30 years probably isn't consulting a chatbot for that. But a Thursday night decision about a Saturday lawn ticket is exactly the moment someone might consult AI.

To those who don't want AI in their lives: The world around us is already being reshaped by it, not just in faraway data centers, but in the systems that underpin how our county already functions.

After all, you can avoid social media in your personal life, but how much does your bank spend on SEO? How many ticket sales for that theater performance came through your local arts organization's Facebook ad budget?

Even people who avoid AI live with its effects. Knowing what's happening matters for all of us: Whether critic or enthusiast, AI is already in your life in a big way.
